name: Valpolicella

climate.koppen_name: Temperate, no dry season, hot summer

terms: Denominazione di Origine Controllata e Garantita, Italy's top tier. Stricter than DOC, and given only to wines that have been DOC for at least seven years.
Denominazione di Origine Controllata. The label names a precise area, and the wine is tested during production.
Indicazione Geografica Tipica, Italy's broad regional tier.
An aged Italian wine. Chianti Riserva needs at least 6 months in barrel and 3 more in bottle before release.
The original heartland of an Italian wine area. In Chianti Classico, members of the producers' consortium carry the black rooster seal.
Valpolicella Superiore made with the partly dried skins left over from Amarone or Recioto.
Valpolicella wines from dried grapes: Amarone is strong and dry, Recioto sweet. Both have been DOCG since 2009.
keyfacts: Valpolicella is a DOC red wine from the province of Verona, authorized in 1968, blended mainly from Corvina and/or Corvinone at 45 to 95% and Rondinella at 5 to 30%.
Classico comes from the zone around Negrar, Marano di Valpolicella, Fumane, Sant'Ambrogio di Valpolicella and San Pietro in Cariano, and Valpantena comes from the Valpantena valley.
Ripasso wine is refermented on the pressed skins left from Recioto or Amarone, then aged in wood, which gives it more structure, alcohol and roundness.
Valpolicella Ripasso is a DOC of its own, and Amarone and Recioto della Valpolicella, made from partly dried grapes, are DOCGs of their own.

notes: Basic Valpolicella is light bodied and fragrant, often served slightly chilled, with sour cherry flavor.
Most has moderate alcohol around 11%, while Amarone and recioto reach 15 to 16%.
Ripasso, steeped on the skins and seeds left from recioto and Amarone, gains alcohol, body, tannin and flavor.
Amarone is rich and full bodied, with notes of mocha, dark chocolate, raisin and dried fig.

blurb.text: A red wine from Verona province in the Veneto. It became a DOC in 1968.
